item.title: Get Started Growing
item.description: Getting started growing cannabis can feel overwhelming, but the fundamentals are straightforward. Keep in mind, all you really need to do is plant a seed. All the variables, and ins and outs, the this and that, it’s all just to maximize your produce. But starting a plant for the love of the plant is as simple as putting a seed in the ground, and letting nature do it’s thing. Cannabis is a hardy, fast-growing plant that thrives in a range of environments. This article covers the basics a first-time grower needs to know.

item.title: Light
item.description:
Light refers to the energy source that drives photosynthesis, which converts light, water, and CO2 into the sugars that plants need to grow. The amount, quality, and duration of light a plant receives directly affects its size, structure, and yield.

Much like other variables involved in growing plants, light can

Sunlight

The sun provides a full spectrum of light that no artificial source can perfectly replicate. Outdoor growers benefit from free, powerful light that naturally shifts in spectrum and duration with the seasons — bluer in summer to promote vegetative growth, redder in autumn to support flowering.

item.title: Nutrients
item.description:
Nutrients are the essential elements that plants absorb through their roots (and to a lesser extent, their leaves) to fuel growth, flowering, and overall health. Understanding what nutrients a plant needs — and when — is one of the key skills in growing cannabis.

Macronutrients (N-P-K)

On most nutrient labels or packages, you’ll often see 3 numbers, like 10-10-10.

These numbers represent the three primary macronutrients used to feed plants: Nitrogen-Phosphorous-Potassium, often referred to as N-P-K (using the element’s periodic table abbreviation).

item.title: Mr. X
item.description: It all began about ten years ago. I had reached a considerably more relaxed period in my life – a time when I had come to feel that there was more to living than science, a time of awakening of my social consciousness and amiability, a time when I was open to new experiences. I had become friendly with a group of people who occasionally smoked cannabis, irregularly, but with evident pleasure. Initially I was unwilling to partake, but the apparent euphoria that cannabis produced and the fact that there was no physiological addiction to the plant eventually persuaded me to try. My initial experiences were entirely disappointing; there was no effect at all, and I began to entertain a variety of hypotheses about cannabis being a placebo which worked by expectation and hyperventilation rather than by chemistry. After about five or six unsuccessful attempts, however, it happened. I was lying on my back in a friend’s living room idly examining the pattern of shadows on the ceiling cast by a potted plant (not cannabis!). I suddenly realized that I was examining an intricately detailed miniature Volkswagen, distinctly outlined by the shadows. I was very skeptical at this perception, and tried to find inconsistencies between Volkswagens and what I viewed on the ceiling. But it was all there, down to hubcaps, license plate, chrome, and even the small handle used for opening the trunk. When I closed my eyes, I was stunned to find that there was a movie going on the inside of my eyelids. Flash . . . a simple country scene with red farmhouse, a blue sky, white clouds, yellow path meandering over green hills to the horizon. . . Flash . . . same scene, orange house, brown sky, red clouds, yellow path, violet fields . . . Flash . . . Flash . . . Flash. The flashes came about once a heartbeat. Each flash brought the same simple scene into view, but each time with a different set of colors . . . exquisitely deep hues, and astonishingly harmonious in their juxtaposition. Since then I have smoked occasionally and enjoyed it thoroughly. It amplifies torpid sensibilities and produces what to me are even more interesting effects, as I will explain shortly.

item.title: Autoflower
item.description:
Autoflower
An autoflowering cannabis plant
Field Value
Origin Cannabis ruderalis hybrids
Flowering trigger Age (not light cycle)
Typical cycle 8–12 weeks seed to harvest
Average height 30–100 cm
Light schedule 18/6 or 20/4 throughout

Autoflowering cannabis refers to varieties that transition from vegetative growth to flowering based on age, rather than a change in photoperiod (light cycle). This trait originates from Cannabis Ruderalis , a species native to regions with short summers and long daylight hours.

item.title: Contributing
item.description:
How to Edit Pages

On each page, you will see an “Edit” link near the top right. If you click on the link, it will take you to a GitHub page where changes can be made.

Requirements

Since the contents of this wiki are stored and hosted on GitHub, you must have a GitHub account to make changes.

Workflow

  1. Click the “Edit” link on any page
  2. Make your changes in the GitHub editor
  3. Changes are made in a branch called Edit
  4. Submit a pull request merging your changes from Edit into Main
  5. Once reviewed and approved, your changes go live

What to Contribute

  • Fix typos and grammatical errors
  • Add missing information to existing articles
  • Create new articles on cannabis-related topics
  • Improve article structure and readability
  • Add sources and citations

Guidelines

  • Keep content factual and well-sourced
  • Use a neutral, encyclopedic tone
  • Follow the Style Guide for formatting
  • Check the Editing Guide for available shortcodes

See Also

  • Editing Guide - Technical reference for Hugo shortcodes
  • Style Guide - Writing conventions

item.title: Editing Guide
item.description:
This site is created using Hugo. When writing pages, there are certain Hugo “shortcodes” that can be used to inject HTML components.

Article Frontmatter

These are the variables that can be provided in frontmatter on each page:

---
title: <Page Title>
description: <Page Description>
draft: false
date: 2026-01-11
lastmod: 2026-01-17
toc: false           <------------Defaults to True; Setting to false will remove the sidebar toc.
categories:
  - <Category Tag>
related:
  - <Related Page 1>
  - <Related Page 2>
aliases:
  - /alternate-url/
---

Shortcodes

toc

This adds a table of contents next to the infobox, in the main/first paragraph of a page. This is useful to fill whitespace. If using this shortcode, it is helpful to set toc: false in the frontmatter of the page.

item.title: Style Guide
item.description:
This guide covers the writing conventions and formatting standards for WeedWeed.Wiki.

For other guidance on contributing and editing, check out:

  • Editing Guide - Technical shortcode reference
  • Contributing - How to contribute

Headers

Use headers to organize content hierarchically:

  • Use ## or <h2> for major sections - displays with a full underline
  • Use ### or <h3> for subsections - displays with a subtle underline under text only
  • Use #### or <h4> for minor subsections - displays with a dotted underline

Cannabinoids are a class of chemical compounds that interact with cannabinoid receptors in the body. They go deeper than just cannabis —your body naturally produces cannabinoids as part of the endocannabinoid system.

item.title: CBD
item.description:
CBD (Cannabidiol)
Chemical structure of CBD
Field Value
Full Name Cannabidiol
Formula C₂₁H₃₀O₂
Molar Mass 314.464 g/mol
Type Cannabinoid
Discovered 1940

Cannabidiol (CBD) is a major phytocannabinoid found in cannabis , accounting for up to 40% of the plant’s extract in some strains. Unlike THC , CBD does not produce psychoactive effects, making it an attractive option for those seeking therapeutic benefits without the “high.”

History

CBD was first isolated in 1940 by American chemist Roger Adams at the University of Illinois. However, its chemical structure wasn’t fully elucidated until 1963 by Raphael Mechoulam and Yuval Shvo in Israel—one year before Mechoulam’s team isolated THC .

Humulene is a monocyclic sesquiterpene found abundantly in hops (Humulus lupulus) and in varying quantities in cannabis . It is responsible for the distinctive earthy, woody aroma associated with beer and contributes to the complex scent profile of many cannabis strains.

item.title: Limonene
item.description:
Limonene
Chemical structure of Limonene
Field Value
Also Known As D-limonene, (+)-limonene
Formula C₁₀H₁₆
Molar Mass 136.238 g/mol
Type Monoterpene
Boiling Point 176°C (349°F)

Limonene is one of the most common terpenes found in nature and the second most abundant terpene in cannabis . It’s responsible for the bright, citrusy aroma found in lemons, oranges, and many uplifting cannabis strains.

Aroma Profile

Limonene produces a distinctive citrus scent:

  • Lemon
  • Orange
  • Grapefruit
  • Tangerine
  • Fresh and zesty

The aroma is often described as bright, clean, and energizing.

item.title: THC
item.description:
THC (Tetrahydrocannabinol)
Chemical structure of THC
Field Value
Full Name Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol
Formula C₂₁H₃₀O₂
Molar Mass 314.469 g/mol
Type Cannabinoid
Discovered 1964

Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), or more precisely Δ9-THC, is the principal psychoactive constituent of cannabis . It is one of at least 113 cannabinoids identified in the plant.

History

THC was first isolated and synthesized in 1964 by Israeli chemist Raphael Mechoulam along with Yechiel Gaoni at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel. This discovery opened the door to understanding how cannabis affects the human body.

item.description:

Cannabis, the most well-known genus in the family

Cannabaceae is a family of flowering plants in the order Rosales. The family is perhaps best known for containing Cannabis , but it also includes hops (Humulus), hackberries (Celtis), and several other genera. Despite the name, the family extends well beyond cannabis — it contains around 11 genera and approximately 120 species.

item.title: Cannabis Ruderalis
item.description:
Cannabis ruderalis
Cannabis ruderalis
Field Value
Kingdom Plantae
Order Rosales
Family Cannabaceae
Genus Cannabis
Species C. ruderalis
Native range Central/Eastern Europe, Russia, Central Asia
Height 30–80 cm
Flowering Autoflowering (age-based)

Cannabis ruderalis is one of three primary species of Cannabis , alongside Cannabis Sativa and Cannabis Indica . It is the smallest and hardiest of the three, and is best known for its autoflowering trait — the ability to flower based on age rather than changes in the light cycle.

item.title: Frequently Asked Questions
item.description:
Consumption

Can cats eat cannabis leaves?

Yes. Leaves are full of nutrients and some cats seem to like them. There is no harm in cats eating your fan leaves.

Why do I get the munchies?

Cannabinoids stimulate the release of a hunger molecule called “ghrelin” . Also food tastes better!

Edibles vs. Smoking

When you inhale cannabis, you are inhaling Delta-9 THC, and goes from lungs to blood stream, so the effects are very quick.

item.title: Pests
item.description:
Pests are an issue that plague all growers. Like most things, an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. Once an infestation gets out of control, it can often be hard to recover.

Common Types of Pests

Aphids

Aphids love to hang out on stems and eat delicious leaves. They are tiny, soft-bodied insects that like to hang out in large groups. They generally amass on stems, or under leaves.

item.title: Cannabis
item.description:
Cannabis
Species of Cannabis
Field Value
Kingdom Plantae
Clade Tracheophytes
Order Rosales
Family Cannabaceae
Genus Cannabis

Cannabis is the “genus” name for the plant that we commonly refer to as “hemp” , “weed”, “cannabis”, “grass”, “marijuana”, and other colloquialisms.

There are a number of “species” that fall under the genus “Cannabis”:

  • Cannabis Sativa
  • Cannabis Indica

Cannabis has been used by humans for thousands of years in industrial, nutritional, and medicinal capacities.

Species of Cannabis
Field Value
Kingdom Plantae
Clade Tracheophytes
Order Rosales

Genus Cannabis

Industrial

Hemp, a variety of Cannabis sativa, is grown for industrial uses including:

  • Fiber production
  • Seed oil extraction
  • Building materials
  • Biofuels
  • Paper

Hemp Uses Throughout History

Herodotus (5th c. BCE, Histories 4.74–75) – describes Scythians using hemp-seed on hot stones in a covered tent (a kind of steam bath / fumigation).

Dioscorides (1st c. CE, De materia medica) – explicitly notes hemp’s everyday utility for “the strongest ropes” and also gives medical notes (e.g., juice instilled for ear issues).

item.title: Photoperiod
item.description:
Photoperiod refers to the duration of light and darkness a plant receives in a 24-hour cycle. In cannabis cultivation, the photoperiod is the primary trigger that tells Cannabis Sativa and Cannabis Indica plants when to transition from vegetative growth to flowering. Plants that depend on this light cycle to flower are called photoperiod plants, in contrast to autoflower varieties which flower based on age.

How It Works

Cannabis is a short-day plant, meaning it flowers when the nights become long enough. In nature, this happens as summer transitions to autumn and daylight hours decrease. The plant detects the length of the uninterrupted dark period — not the light period — through photoreceptor proteins called phytochromes.
